summary: Brian argues investors are fixated on which company builds the winning humanoid robot while the smarter play is owning the suppliers every robot needs, and he walks the full bill of materials. His one outright buy is Regal Rexnord (RRX, BUY): it builds the entire robot joint — servo motors, micro motors, ball screws and precision gears — under one roof, a real cash-generating business that looks expensive at 49x trailing earnings only because of Altra-deal amortization, trading closer to 15x next year's profit with a PEG near 1. On the watch list pending better prices: Timken (TKR, CONDITIONAL_BUY), the only US-listed maker of both strain-wave and cycloidal reducers; Allegro MicroSystems (ALGM, CONDITIONAL_BUY), whose sensor content per machine rises ~30x from robot vacuum to humanoid but sits at its richest valuation ever; Novanta (NOVT, CONDITIONAL_BUY), the force-sensing leader now partnered with Nvidia; and Cognex (CGNX, CONDITIONAL_BUY), the machine-vision leader recovering on warehouse automation. Nvidia (NVDA, HOLD) he frames as the robot 'brain' on both the device (Jetson Thor) and training side — a name he has long championed, not a new buy here. Speculative or watch-only names — MP Materials (MP), Vishay Precision (VPG), Moog (MOG.A), plus OTC names Harmonic Drive (6324.T), Nabtesco (6472.T) and Melexis (MLXSF) — are all UNCERTAIN. He warns most of the basket has run hot on hype and demands entry discipline.
title: Everyone's Watching AI. They're Missing This
